channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: Betty Boop, Blondie and three classic detectives enter the public domain
item.description: Works first published in 1930 are now free of U.S. copyright, including early Betty Boop and Blondie appearances, nine Mickey Mouse cartoons and the book debuts of Nancy Drew, Sam Spade and Miss Marple. The annual release offers a rich field for copyright archaeology, preservation and new editions—while later character elements can remain protected.

item.title: Russian strikes put Ukraine's independent publishers at risk
item.description: Russian attacks have destroyed more than 13 million Ukrainian books and crucial printing infrastructure, including eight million books at publisher Ranok's warehouse. Small presses and debut authors are especially exposed, making proposed grants, state purchases and war-risk insurance consequential for literary diversity and cultural survival.

item.title: What WordPress's release scanning catches—and what it cannot
item.description: WordPress.org now scans each plugin and theme release during a cooldown and blocks high-risk updates before distribution. This practical guide explains the boundary that matters: the gate can examine a new release, but it cannot protect an already installed vulnerable or compromised plugin. It then maps the remaining site-owner defenses.

item.title: The webhooks family tree begins with rssCloud and weblog pings
item.description: Quentin Mousset traces webhooks to blog-era protocols: rssCloud in 2000, weblogs.com pings in 2001, and TrackBack and Pingback in 2002. The article carefully separates surviving evidence from uncertain lore, including a lost 2006 “Web hooks” post, while following the same HTTP callback pattern through WebSub and today's agent protocols.

item.title: Untangling Blue Beetle's public-domain claims
item.description: Comics editor David Mariotte examines why public-domain claims around Blue Beetle require more than finding old issues without notices. He distinguishes Dan Garret from DC's later Dan Garrett and Ted Kord versions, considers Charlton's 1983 sale to DC, and separates copyright in particular stories from character elements and trademarks.

item.title: WordPress takes the lead at the Open Website Alliance
item.description: WordPress Foundation executive director Mary Hubbard has become president of the Open Website Alliance, a rotating role among WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and TYPO3. The group advocates for open-source publishing and shares practices across projects, including work on European security rules affecting community-built content-management systems.

item.title: WordPress 7.1.2 fixes a critical security flaw
item.description: WordPress 7.1.2 is a security-only release fixing one critical vulnerability. The project recommends updating sites immediately; installations that support automatic background updates should receive it without manual intervention.

item.title: Jack Kirby's Lower East Side roots get a street and exhibition
item.description: New York co-named an intersection Jack Kirby Way near the comics legend's childhood home. A free American Jewish Historical Society exhibition, open through Nov. 26, pairs the tribute with rare comics and original art tracing how the Lower East Side shaped Kirby's imagination.

item.title: A free doorway into 11,000 classic pulp magazines
item.description: Open Culture tours the Pulp Magazine Archive, a huge collection of digitized science-fiction, fantasy and detective magazines. The scans preserve stories, illustrations and advertising from publishing's pulp era, making the collection useful both for casual reading and copyright archaeology.

item.title: Clover Press revives Marvel Masterworks
item.description: Clover Press is bringing back Marvel Masterworks with new restorations, three cover choices per volume and collectible extras. A Kickstarter launches the line with Uncanny X-Men Vol. 18, Super-Villain Team-Up Vol. 1, The Mighty Thor Vol. 25 and The Tomb of Dracula Vol. 6. Longtime Marvel editor Cory Sedlmeier remains series steward.

item.title: Podium acquisition shows the value of indie authors
item.description: Flexpoint Ford and Shamrock Capital acquired audiobook-focused Podium Entertainment, whose 15,000-title catalog emphasizes genre fiction and authors who began by self-publishing. Podium first drew attention by producing the audiobook of Andy Weir's The Martian. The new owners also plan an employee ownership program.

item.title: Jacksonville library opens a century of newspapers online
item.description: Jacksonville Public Library has expanded free online access to three local newspaper archives: the Florida Times-Union from 1883 to today, the Beaches Leader from 1963 and the Jacksonville Journal from 1901 to 1988. Cardholders can search full pages, photos, cartoons and ads—rich primary material for local history and genealogy.

item.title: Major software firms pledge more support for public package registries
item.description: GitHub, Google, IBM, Microsoft and Sonatype have joined an OpenSSF pledge to help fund package registries such as Maven Central, npm and PyPI. These lightly staffed services handle trillions of downloads while facing rising security and infrastructure costs. The plan targets enterprise customers while keeping access free for developers and small organizations.

item.title: Kim Stanley Robinson keeps returning to the hardest chapter of his climate novel
item.description: Kim Stanley Robinson has discussed The Ministry for the Future in more than 600 talks, but he still will not read its harrowing opening heat-wave chapter aloud. The 74-year-old science-fiction author explains why he set the scene in India, responds to criticism of the novel and describes the persistence behind his guarded optimism.

item.title: Jacksonville lands among Oxford Economics' five U.S. cities to watch
item.description: Oxford Economics named Jacksonville one of five U.S. cities to watch, citing its fast growth, transportation links, business climate and expanding finance, logistics and technology sectors. The assessment also flags familiar pressures: infrastructure, housing affordability and the need for enough skilled workers to sustain the city's momentum.
